title: Iran Rejects Trump Ceasefire as US Strikes Enter Third Week, Shipping Routes Choked
excerpt: Tehran dismisses latest peace proposal as a 'temporary deal' while Houthi blockade and Strait of Hormuz closure trap Saudi oil exports, sending Brent crude above $91.
body:
• Iran rejected a ceasefire proposal delivered by Iraqi PM Ali al-Zaidi on behalf of President Trump, calling it a "temporary deal" that fails to resolve control of the Strait of Hormuz.
  • US forces have conducted 13 consecutive nights of airstrikes on Iranian targets, killing 50 civilians and wounding 500, while 18 US service members have died since the war began in February.
  • Houthi rebels imposed a naval blockade on Saudi shipping through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, forcing oil tankers to reverse course and threatening to cut 7% of global oil supply.
  • Brent crude has surged past $91 a barrel and US gasoline prices are back above $4 a gallon amid the escalation.

Iran on Thursday rejected a new ceasefire proposal presented by Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who carried the deal from Washington after meeting President Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Iranian officials described the offer as the "only offer on the table" but dismissed it as a "temporary deal" that failed to address the central dispute over control of the Strait of Hormuz, according to the New York Times.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, lead negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met with the Iraqi delegation in Tehran. Araghchi said on state television that al-Zaidi had shared his "views and impressions" from Washington but argued that additional mediators were unnecessary.

"The problem is not passing messages. The problem is America's outlook, which is illogical, greedy and controlling."

— Abbas Araghchi, Iranian Foreign Minister

Thirteen Nights of Strikes and Counting

The rejection came as US Central Command confirmed its 13th consecutive night of airstrikes on Iran, targeting military command centres, maritime capabilities, missile launch sites, and air defence systems across the country's south and west. Explosions were reported near Shiraz, Konarak, and Chabahar in southern Iran, as well as a civilian site outside Abdanan in the west, according to Iranian state media.

An Iranian health ministry official said the recent US strikes had killed 50 civilians and wounded 500. On the American side, Trump confirmed that 18 US service members have been killed since the conflict began on February 28. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told senators the war has cost $37.5 billion and requested $70 billion in supplemental funding to replenish depleted missile supplies, according to Reuters.

Trump, meanwhile, escalated his rhetoric. "I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than anything we have ever had before. I am close to making a decision," he told Israel's Channel 12. He also renewed threats to strike Iran's Natanz nuclear facility and vowed on Truth Social to "bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT" for every ship Iran attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.

Two Chokepoints Under Siege

The conflict has now disrupted shipping through both of the world's most critical energy chokepoints simultaneously. The Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps declared the Strait of Hormuz "completely closed" after a blast in the channel, stopping three oil tankers — one set ablaze and two forced to turn back through mined waters.

Just four commodity vessels crossed the strait on Monday, down from seven the previous day, according to Kpler data. The maritime security agency UKMTO reported a tanker struck by a projectile, forcing its crew to abandon ship.

Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen opened a second front by imposing a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia through the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea. Two oil tankers carrying Saudi crude bound for China and India reversed course on Tuesday rather than risk passage, according to Reuters. British maritime risk group Vanguard called it the "first confirmed changes to commercial tanker routing" following the embargo.

A full closure of the Bab al-Mandab could reduce global oil supply by 7%, trapping most Saudi oil exports, according to analysts. Brent crude has climbed above $91 a barrel, with US gasoline prices back over $4 a gallon.

Iran Strikes Across the Gulf

Iran launched retaliatory attacks against US assets across the region. The Revolutionary Guards said they targeted Amazon's regional data centre infrastructure in Bahrain, struck accommodation facilities used by US military personnel at Bahrain's Sheikh Isa Air Base, and launched drone attacks against three US military bases in Kuwait, according to Iranian state media. Jordan's armed forces intercepted and destroyed five Iranian drones.

Attacks on Kuwaiti power and water desalination plants have raised alarms about critical infrastructure in desert nations that depend on desalination for potable water.

What This Means for Indian Interests

The simultaneous choking of both major shipping routes carries direct consequences for India, which sources roughly 60% of its crude oil from the Gulf. The reversal of Saudi tankers bound for India and China signals potential supply disruptions that could push Indian fuel prices higher. Millions of Indian workers in Gulf nations, particularly in Bahrain, Kuwait, and the UAE, face growing security risks as the conflict spills across borders. India's diplomatic efforts through its relationship with both Washington and Tehran will face increasing pressure as the conflict widens.

Diplomacy has not entirely collapsed. Iran's Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni visited Pakistan, a key mediator, to urge continued peace efforts. But with Trump weighing an even larger military operation and Iran showing no willingness to accept anything short of a comprehensive deal, the path to de-escalation appears narrow.

The US House of Representatives passed a War Powers resolution on Wednesday, with four Republicans joining Democrats to rebuke the president over the unauthorized military campaign — a sign of growing domestic unease with a conflict now approaching its fifth month.
